Type II Error and Sample Size for a One Sample, One Sided z Test

Source: R/power.R
power_z.Rd

For the one sample, upper tailed z test of \(H_0\!: \mu = \mu_0\) against \(H_1\!: \mu = \mu_1 > \mu_0\) with a known population standard deviation, returns either the sample size needed for a chosen Type II error rate, the Type II error rate at a chosen sample size, or a table of Type II error rates over a range of sample sizes. Power is one minus the Type II error rate. The function is named power_z so as not to mask stats::power.

Usage

power_z(
  mu_0,
  mu_1,
  sigma,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  n = NULL,
  n_min = NULL,
  n_max = NULL,
  n_values = NULL,
  beta = NULL,
  method = c("sample_size", "type_2", "type_2_seq")
)

Arguments

mu_0

The population mean under the null hypothesis. A single number.

mu_1

The population mean under the alternative hypothesis. A single number greater than mu_0.

sigma

The known population standard deviation. A single positive number.

conf_level

One minus the one-sided Type I error rate, strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95, a test at the 0.05 level.

n

For method = "type_2": the sample size at which to compute the Type II error rate. A whole number of at least 1.

n_min, n_max

For method = "type_2_seq": the smallest and largest sample sizes of the table. Whole numbers with n_max >= n_min >= 1.

n_values

For method = "type_2_seq": the number of sample sizes in the table. They are equally spaced from n_min to n_max, and each is taken to the nearest whole number (a value halfway between two whole numbers goes to the larger); duplicates are dropped, so the table can have fewer rows than n_values. When n_values is at least the number of whole sample sizes from n_min to n_max, the table has every one of them.

beta

For method = "sample_size": the target Type II error rate (one minus the desired power), strictly between 0 and 1.

method

What to compute: "sample_size", which needs beta; "type_2", which needs n; or "type_2_seq", which needs n_min, n_max, and n_values. When method is not given, it is the method whose arguments are supplied (beta alone, n alone, or the three grid arguments); supplying arguments for more than one result without naming method is an error. When method is given, arguments it does not use are ignored. A unique abbreviation of a method name is accepted; NULL is the same as not giving method.

Value

Depends on method:

"sample_size"

A length one integer: the smallest sample size whose Type II error rate is at most beta (\(n_\beta\) of Details, rounded up).

"type_2"

A length one number: the Type II error rate \(\beta(n)\).

"type_2_seq"

A data.frame with one row per sample size and two columns: n (integer, the sample size) and type_2_error (the Type II error rate \(\beta(n)\)).

Details

The test rejects \(H_0\) when \(\sqrt{n}\,(\bar{X} - \mu_0)/\sigma > z_{1-\alpha}\), with one-sided Type I error rate \(\alpha = 1 - \) conf_level. Its Type II error rate at \(\mu = \mu_1\) with \(n\) observations is $$\beta(n) = \Phi\!\left(z_{1-\alpha} - \sqrt{n}\,\frac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{\sigma}\right),$$ and the sample size at which it equals a target \(\beta\) is $$n_\beta = \left(\frac{(z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta})\,\sigma} {\mu_1 - \mu_0}\right)^2.$$ \(n_\beta\) is rarely a whole number. method = "sample_size" returns the smallest whole sample size whose Type II error rate \(\beta(n)\) is at most beta, which is \(n_\beta\) rounded up. (When \(n_\beta\) is within rounding error of a whole number, \(\beta(n)\) decides between that number and the next, so asking for the Type II error rate that this function reports at \(n\) returns \(n\).) When beta is at least conf_level (a power no greater than the Type I error rate) every sample size meets the target and 1 is returned.

Only the upper tailed alternative is computed, so mu_1 must exceed mu_0. For a lower tailed alternative the results are the same with both means reflected: pass -mu_0 and -mu_1. For an unknown standard deviation, two groups, or a two-sided test, use the planning functions in DMAR, for example ss_power_smd.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

ss_power_smd in DMAR for two groups with an unknown standard deviation.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# A training program is expected to raise the mean score on a
# standardized assessment from 100 to 104; the standard deviation of
# the assessment is known to be 15.

# Sample size for a Type II error rate of 0.20 (power 0.80)
power_z(mu_0 = 100, mu_1 = 104, sigma = 15, beta = 0.20)
#> [1] 87

# Type II error rate with 60 trainees
power_z(mu_0 = 100, mu_1 = 104, sigma = 15, n = 60)
#> [1] 0.3369734

# Type II error rates for 20 to 140 trainees
power_z(mu_0 = 100, mu_1 = 104, sigma = 15, n_min = 20, n_max = 140,
        n_values = 7)
#>     n type_2_error
#> 1  20   0.67446781
#> 2  40   0.48337114
#> 3  60   0.33697339
#> 4  80   0.22956337
#> 5 100   0.15343470
#> 6 120   0.10091885
#> 7 140   0.06547211
